title: Three o'clock
hook: the hour of Christ's death, kept as an hour of mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Mercy chaplet: an offering to the Father, and a plea for the whole world. Your line was have mercy on us.

In Acts, Peter and John are walking up to the Temple in the middle of the afternoon. Not to preach, but to pray, at an hour set aside for it. At the gate, a man who has never walked asks them for money. The same hour turns up in the Gospels, on an afternoon when, Mark says, darkness covered the land. And some Catholics still mark it, by the clock, every day.
screen: `PETER AND JOHN GO UP TO PRAY.` → `AN HOUR SET ASIDE.` → `STILL MARKED BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Gospels count the day's hours from morning, so their ninth hour falls in the middle of the afternoon, and Catholic tradition keeps it at three. Acts says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer." An hour of prayer, already, before it meant anything more. Mark tells of darkness over the land from the sixth hour until the ninth, and places Jesus's death at the ninth. Luke gives his last words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Then he breathes his last. For Christians, the afternoon hour of prayer became the hour he died. The Church's own prayer kept the hour. The Liturgy of the Hours has a short mid-afternoon office called None, the ninth. Monks and sisters stop their work for it; so do some lay people with a prayer book in a desk drawer. Then the hour of mercy. In her diary, Faustina wrote that Jesus asked her to honor the hour of his death, at three o'clock, and to ask then for mercy, especially for sinners. She records that even a brief moment was enough: a thought of the cross while carrying on with her work. So in some Catholic hospitals and parishes, a bell or a voice marks three. Some people pray the chaplet then. Some pause for a few seconds at a desk, in traffic, in a checkout line. None of it is required. That's the shape of a devotion: an ordinary minute of an ordinary afternoon, turned toward one afternoon on a hill outside Jerusalem.
screen: `THE NINTH HOUR: MID-AFTERNOON.` · `THE HOUR JESUS DIED.` · `NONE: THE CHURCH'S AFTERNOON PRAYER.` · `FAUSTINA: THE HOUR OF MERCY.` · then, large: `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Think of where you'll be at three this afternoon, a desk, a kitchen, a car, and choose one tiny sign for that moment: setting down whatever's in your hands, one slow breath, the sign of the cross. If you pray, borrow Jesus's words from Luke, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit, or ask mercy for someone who's suffering; if you don't, let three o'clock be a moment to remember that person.
Three o'clock. The ninth hour: an old hour of prayer, the hour the Gospels give for Jesus's death, and in Faustina's devotion, the hour of mercy.
Your line: the hour of mercy. Even a brief moment, Faustina wrote, was enough. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Catholics pause at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition gives for Jesus's death, to pray the Divine Mercy chaplet or simply to remember the cross; religious communities pray the mid-afternoon hour of the Liturgy of the Hours.

chat.meaning: Mark places Jesus's death at the ninth hour, mid-afternoon. Faustina wrote of honoring three o'clock as the hour of mercy, and the pause is never required.

notes: The equation of the Gospels' ninth hour with about three in the afternoon (hours counted from roughly 6 a.m.) is stated as how the Gospels count and as what tradition keeps; confirm the phrasing.
Mark 15:33–34 gives darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour and the cry at the ninth hour; Jesus's death follows (15:37). Confirm 'places Jesus's death at the ninth' is fair.

Faustina's Diary (e.g. on the hour of mercy, asking mercy especially for sinners, and that even a brief moment suffices) paraphrased; the English translation is under copyright. Confirm the paragraphs and summary.
'None, the ninth' names the mid-afternoon hour (nona hora); confirm wording. Under the current Liturgy of the Hours the daytime hour may be said at mid-morning, midday or mid-afternoon.
Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 3:1 and Luke 23:46: confirm.
